items.title: Herpetologist Answers Snake Questions
items.description:
Reptile expert Frank Burbrink joins WIRED to answer the internet’s burning questions about snakes. What’s the most venomous snake? How do snakes hear? How accurate is _Snakes on a Plane?_ Answers to these questions and many more await on Snake Support.

WIRED recommends:
https://youtu.be/4kyBn6-WNTk
https://youtu.be/y66Hw3sevuc
https://youtu.be/2YquYkNcF7I

Watch more from WIRED | Tech Support: https://www.youtube.com/show/VLPLibNZv5Zd0dwIx8baZGDdkoPNg6LHAPDi?sbp=QAE%3D

#Snake #Reptiles #Cobra
items.why_watch: Frank Burbrink is a working herpetologist at the American Museum of Natural History, so his answers carry real scientific weight rather than casual enthusiast knowledge. The format moves briskly through genuinely interesting questions — snake hearing mechanisms, venom rankings, and whether Hollywood gets anything right — without lingering too long on any one topic. If you've ever had a snake question you were too embarrassed to Google seriously, this covers it with good humor and actual expertise.

items.why_watch: Max Miller traces potted meat back to 18th-century British preservation techniques, explaining the practical logic of fat sealing as a refrigeration substitute before anyone had refrigerators. He cooks a period-accurate recipe on camera, so you see exactly how the method works rather than just reading about it. It's a useful reframe for anyone interested in fermentation or preservation — these weren't desperate measures, they were deliberate, sophisticated food science.

items.why_watch: This episode puts the 1915 Battle of the Gulf of Riga under a counterfactual lens — asking what a different outcome might have changed about the Eastern Front and WWI's broader trajectory. At over an hour it's a genuine deep-dive, better suited to a long walk than casual background listening. If you find the Eastern Front underexamined compared to the Western, this is exactly the kind of niche, thoughtful analysis that rewards the time investment.

items.why_watch: This is a warmly shot travel vlog centered on Taormina in high summer — birthdays, a babymoon, and the specific golden-hour light that makes Sicily look almost unreasonable. Lois films with a candid, unhurried eye rather than trying to produce a destination guide, so it reads more like a friend's holiday footage than a tourism ad. discovery_articles.title: John Ford Statue in Portland, Maine
discovery_articles.snippet: If you asked John Ford what he did with his life, he'd tell you he made westerns. If you asked anyone else, they'd tell you he transformed the art of cinema. John Ford is a name as much as an idea.

discovery_articles.title: Must-Try Spots For Noodle Lovers
discovery_articles.snippet: Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In fact, noodles would go on to become inextricable from ancient Chinese culture, with a wheat-based version emerging as a staple of the Han dynasty. Centuries later, noodle-making would hit Europe, transforming the cuisines of Italy during the Middle Ages and Germany in the early 18th century.

discovery_articles.title: Waldkunstpfad in Darmstadt, Germany
discovery_articles.snippet: Hidden in the forest on the southern edge of Darmstadt, the Waldkunstpfad turns an ordinary woodland walk into something considerably more surreal. Along the trails, artworks emerge between the trees, lean against trunks, occupy clearings, or use the forest itself as part of the installation. Instead of entering a gallery, visitors simply follow the path and wait to see what the woods have decided to reveal.

garden_note.note: September arrives in Zürich with that particular golden-hour haze that makes the allotments along the Limmat look like oil paintings — the dahlias are at their most unapologetic, and the first windfalls are already scenting the grass beneath the apple trees. Step outside before the dew settles and listen: the swallows are quietly rehearsing their goodbyes.
